All three losses are trained on the same triples: a prompt $x$, a preferred response $y_w$ and a dispreferred one $y_l$. They differ in two things: what they treat as a response's score (its "reward"), and what they ask the gap between the two scores to do.

A shorthand used below (ours, not the papers'): $h = \log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w|x)} - \log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l|x)}$. In words, $h$ is how much more the policy has raised the winner's likelihood relative to the loser's, compared with the reference model. The IPO paper calls this $h_\pi(y_w, y_l)$ ([IPO, p. 5](http://pdf.invalid/llm/post-training/preference-learning/A%20General%20Theoretical%20Paradigm%20to%20Understand%20Learning%20from%20Human%20Preferences.pdf?dest=subsection.5.1&page=5)).

## DPO: logistic loss on the reference-relative gap

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}} = -\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_w,y_l)\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\log\sigma\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w|x)} - \beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l|x)}\right)\right] = -\mathbb{E}\left[\log\sigma(\beta h)\right]$$

([DPO, p. 4, Eq. 7](http://pdf.invalid/llm/post-training/preference-learning/Direct%20Preference%20Optimization.%20Your%20Language%20Model%20is%20Secretly%20a%20Reward%20Model.pdf?dest=section.4&page=4))

- **Where it comes from.** The best policy under the KL-regularised RLHF objective is $\pi_r \propto \pi_{\text{ref}}\exp(r/\beta)$ (Eq. 4). Turned around, this gives the reward $r = \beta\log\frac{\pi_r}{\pi_{\text{ref}}} + \beta\log Z(x)$ (Eq. 5). Plugging that into the Bradley–Terry model, where only reward differences matter, cancels $Z(x)$. The reward-model loss then becomes a loss on the policy itself (p. 4).
- **What a step does.** The gradient raises the winner's likelihood and lowers the loser's. Each pair is weighted by $\sigma(\hat r(y_l) - \hat r(y_w))$, i.e. by how wrongly the implicit reward currently orders the pair. Dropping this weight makes the model degenerate (p. 4).

## IPO: squared loss toward a fixed target gap

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{IPO}} = \mathbb{E}_{(y_w,y_l)\sim D}\left[\left(h_\pi(y_w,y_l) - \frac{\tau^{-1}}{2}\right)^2\right]$$

([IPO, p. 6, Eq. 17](http://pdf.invalid/llm/post-training/preference-learning/A%20General%20Theoretical%20Paradigm%20to%20Understand%20Learning%20from%20Human%20Preferences.pdf?dest=subsection.5.2&page=6)). Here $\tau$ is the KL coefficient, the role $\beta$ plays in DPO; the IPO paper writes DPO with $\tau$ (p. 3, Eq. 4).

- **Where it comes from.** IPO is a special case of a general objective, ΨPO: maximise $\mathbb{E}[\Psi(p^*(y\succ y'))] - \tau D_{\text{KL}}(\pi\|\pi_{\text{ref}})$ (p. 3, Eq. 6). With $\Psi(q)=\log\frac{q}{1-q}$, ΨPO has the same optimal policy as RLHF and DPO (p. 4, Prop. 1). IPO instead sets $\Psi$ to the identity (p. 5, Eq. 8).
- **Why DPO overfits.** If $y$ always beats $y'$, Bradley–Terry needs $r(y)-r(y')\to\infty$, so $\pi^*(y')=0$ whatever $\tau$ is: the KL term stops working. With little data, a true preference of 0.8 can easily be estimated as 1 (p. 4, §4.2).
- **What IPO does instead.** The loss is a regression of the log-ratio gap onto a finite target, $\frac{1}{2\tau}$. So it always pulls the solution back toward $\pi_{\text{ref}}$, whereas DPO keeps pushing the gap up (p. 6). To get Eq. 17, each pair is used in both orders, which lowers variance, and the result is simplified up to a constant (p. 6).
- **Evidence.** IPO is supported only by toy bandit examples, with no LLM experiments (p. 7–8).

## SimPO: logistic loss on length-normalised log-likelihoods, with a margin, no reference model

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{SimPO}} = -\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_w,y_l)\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\log\sigma\left(\frac{\beta}{|y_w|}\log\pi_\theta(y_w|x) - \frac{\beta}{|y_l|}\log\pi_\theta(y_l|x) - \gamma\right)\right]$$

([SimPO, p. 4, Eq. 6](http://pdf.invalid/llm/post-training/preference-learning/SimPO.%20Simple%20Preference%20Optimization%20with%20a%20Reference-Free%20Reward.pdf?dest=subsection.2.3&page=4))

- **The reward.** It is $r_{\text{SimPO}} = \frac{\beta}{|y|}\log\pi_\theta(y|x)$, the average per-token log-probability (p. 3, Eq. 4).
- **Why drop the reference model.** It costs memory and compute. More importantly, DPO's reward differs from the likelihood used at generation time: after DPO training, only about 50% of training triples have the winner ahead on average log-likelihood (p. 3).
- **Why average rather than sum.** A summed log-probability gives a length bias (p. 3). Removing the length normalisation leads to long, low-quality outputs (p. 3).
- **The margin.** $\gamma > 0$ asks the winner's reward to beat the loser's by at least $\gamma$ (p. 3, Eq. 5). Quality first improves as $\gamma$ grows, then degrades if it gets too large (p. 3).
- **No KL term.** The authors credit three things with keeping the drift from the reference low: a small learning rate, diverse preference data, and the robustness of LLMs (p. 4).
- **Settings.** The recommended values are β = 2.0–2.5 and γ = 0.5–1.5 (p. 4). This β only scales the reward; it is not a KL coefficient.

## Side by side

| | DPO | IPO | SimPO |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reward of a response | $\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta}{\pi_{\text{ref}}}$ (p. 4) | log-ratio vs. $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ inside $h_\pi$ (p. 5) | $\frac{\beta}{\lvert y\rvert}\log\pi_\theta$ (p. 3) |
| Reference model | yes | yes | no (p. 3) |
| Loss shape | $-\log\sigma(\cdot)$ | squared error $(\cdot - \text{target})^2$ | $-\log\sigma(\cdot - \gamma)$ |
| What happens to the gap | keeps growing; with deterministic preferences, $\pi(y_l)\to 0$ for any β (IPO paper, p. 4) | pulled to $\frac{1}{2\tau}$, overshoot is penalised (p. 6) | pushed past the margin γ (p. 3) |
| Length normalisation | no | no | yes (p. 3) |

The SimPO paper's baseline table writes IPO as $\left(\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w|x)} - \log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l|x)} - \frac{1}{2\tau}\right)^2$ ([SimPO, p. 5, Table 3](http://pdf.invalid/llm/post-training/preference-learning/SimPO.%20Simple%20Preference%20Optimization%20with%20a%20Reference-Free%20Reward.pdf?dest=table.3&page=5)), which matches the IPO paper's Eq. 17. SimPO's authors note that IPO also has a target margin, but find its full objective less effective (p. 3).

**What the margin does in each (our reading of the formulas, not stated in the papers).** Take a pair the model already orders correctly by a lot:
- DPO and SimPO both use a logistic loss, so the gradient there shrinks toward zero but never changes sign. They keep pushing the gap up, ever more weakly. SimPO's γ only moves the point where the push weakens.
- IPO's squared loss reverses sign once $h > \frac{1}{2\tau}$. It actively pulls an over-separated pair back. That is the mechanism behind its "always regularises toward $\pi_{\text{ref}}$" claim.

I read the three papers' markdown and their notes; all are converted from arXiv's HTML and none has an open conversion issue. I didn't change anything, so there's no commit message. I can add this comparison to the Q&A in the three notes if you'd like.
